newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli Treasury head says tax model flawed.
newsitem.headline: Israeli Treasury head says tax model flawed.

text.p: The head of Israel's Treasury said in an interview published on Friday the government's method for projecting tax revenues was flawed and outdated.

David Brodet, the director-general of the Treasury, told Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper the government's budget deficit reaching 1.28 billion shekels in January was caused not only by a slowdown in the economy but by the Treasury's own failure.

"We have stumbled and failed," Brodet said. "Our tax model on which we base our projections is too old, insensitive to the deep changes in the Israeli economy since the early 1990s. Since then the economy grew 50 percent."
Israel's 1997 budget calls for a deficit of 9.7 billion shekels, or 2.8 percent of gross domestic product. But the January figures and early figures for February cast doubt on meeting that target.

A senior Bank of Israel official called for a further budget cut of two billion shekels. The bank's director of research Leo Lederman said in a separate interview to Yedioth Ahronoth he was worried by the growing deficit.

"What we already know about January and February is very negative," he said. "There are very large excesses in the budget. It is necessary to prepare a plan recommending cuts of at least two billion shekels before it is too late."
Lederman recommended cutting expenditures without increasing taxes. He warned if the cuts weren't made not only would Israel's economy suffer but its international credit rating could be hurt too.

"If in 1997 for the third year in a row the deficit exceeds (the target), then not only will the uncertainty in the economy grow and growth be damaged but I warn that Israel's international credit rating could be hurt," he said.
